content: In physical chemistry, saturation refers to the point at which a solution of a substance can no longer dissolve additional amounts of that substance. Beyond this point, any extra substance will form a precipitate. This saturation point is influenced by the temperature of the liquid and the chemical properties of the substances involved. This principle is utilized in recrystallization processes to purify chemicals. A substance is dissolved in a hot solvent until it reaches saturation, and as the solvent cools, its solubility decreases, causing the excess solute to precipitate. Impurities, present in much lower concentrations, remain dissolved in the liquid because they do not saturate the solvent. If the concentration of a solution exceeds the saturation point, often due to cooling, the solution becomes supersaturated. In the context of surface processes in physical chemistry, saturation describes the extent to which a binding site is fully occupied. For instance, base saturation refers to the proportion of exchangeable cations that are base cations. Similarly, in environmental soil science, nitrogen saturation occurs when an ecosystem, such as soil, can no longer store additional nitrogen. In organic chemistry, a saturated compound is one that contains no double or triple bonds. For example, in saturated linear hydrocarbons, each carbon atom is bonded to two hydrogen atoms, except for the terminal carbons, which are bonded to three hydrogen atoms. In the case of methane, a saturated compound, the central carbon atom is bonded to four hydrogen atoms. Alkanes are examples of saturated hydrocarbons, while alkenes are unsaturated. The degree of unsaturation indicates the amount of hydrogen a compound can bind. This terminology is also applied to the fatty acid components of lipids, where fats are classified as saturated or unsaturated based on the presence of carbon-carbon double bonds in their fatty acid chains. Unsaturated structures contain double or occasionally triple bonds. Many vegetable oils contain fatty acids with one (monounsaturated) or more (polyunsaturated) double bonds. The bromine number is a measure of unsaturation. In organometallic chemistry, an unsaturated complex has fewer than 18 valence electrons, making it susceptible to oxidative addition or coordination with an additional ligand. Unsaturation is a common feature of many catalysts, as it is often necessary for substrate activation. In biochemistry, saturation refers to the fraction of total protein binding sites that are occupied at any given time.
